lines.note: Meitet denotes an eminent learned person, equated with Meixǒ and glossed as a celebrated scholar. Final t is the historical checked-syllable spelling, not an omitted tçu; Vt is italic.
The example contrasts investigating old things with knowing new ones. Furuqiuo and ataraxiqiuo contain the attached object particle; the statement continues with the scholar’s preference below.
Meitetno conomu tocoro nari completes the statement that this is what a learned person delights in. Taif. is the upright source label; italic Lib. introduces the next row’s book number.
The scan reads book 28, not the OCR mixture a8. The Portuguese begins “to investigate old things and know”; saber is divided after ſa without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ber as nouas he couſa que os letrados apetecem.

lines.note: Ber completes saber. The remainder says that knowing new things is something scholars desire, matching the Japanese contrast between old and new rather than adding another entry.
Meitocu concerns outstanding qualities and virtues. Grandes partes and calidades describe personal excellence, not physical parts; the list continues below.

Virtudes completes the gloss. Meitocuno cunxi is a virtuous gentleman, paraphrased by Tocuno aru cunxi across the break. The damaged e in Meitocuno replaces OCR Maitocuno and agrees with the headword and later repetition.
Cuno completes Tocuno; the synonym means a gentleman possessed of virtue. The Portuguese begins a virtuous man with good qualities, completed below.
Boas partes finishes the virtuous-man gloss. The next example begins with the same virtuous gentleman as subject and tenca, the realm; its object particle is on the following row.
Uo tamotçu completes “maintains the realm.” The Portuguese calls the person prudent and virtuous; virtuo continues as ſo below without a securely printed hyphen.

runs.text: ſo ſoſtenta, & tem mão no imperio.

lines.note: The ruler sustains the empire and keeps control of it. Initial ſo completes virtuoſo; ſoſtenta and mão remain as printed rather than being modernized.
Meiuacu is affliction or distress here, not only modern inconvenience. Vt introduces Meiuacu xenban nari, with the headword physically divided after Mei.
Meiuacu xenban nari intensifies the distress; the Portuguese correspondingly gives very great affliction. Affli- has a visible terminal mark and continues below.
Ção completes afflição, followed by pena, pain or sorrow. This short continuation closes the intensified example rather than forming a separate entry.

runs.text: Couſa que cauſa ſentimento, ou dà

lines.note: Meiuacuna describes something causing distress or giving affliction. Both Portuguese alternatives share the continuation on the next row.
Afflição completes dà afflição and closes the Meiuacuna gloss. The brief printed row remains separate; nothing from the following headword is imported into it.
Meiuan is paraphrased as a tea bowl, Chano chauan. The Portuguese identifies a porcelain drinking vessel; Porſolana retains the printed historical form, and be- continues below.
Ber completes beber. Cha is italic here, like the surrounding gloss, while Meiuanni muneuo ſuſugu is roman; the example describes refreshing or rinsing the breast with tea.

runs.text: Com hũa vez de Cha refreſcar o estamago, ou

lines.note: The translation describes refreshing the stomach or breast with a serving of tea. Hũa, supported by the compressed a type also visible in Cha, replaces OCR hũs; the second Cha has a capital C.
O peito supplies “the breast,” completing the alternative to the stomach. Terminal S. is an upright written-usage label, separate from the italic Portuguese explanation.
Meiuǒ is explained through Naqu camome, a gull that cries or sings. Q̃ and cãta remain unexpanded abbreviations, and final S. is the written-usage label.
Mei vn is a bright or clear cloud. The space within the headword is visibly present and is not removed to produce a modern-looking single lexical form.

Meixei denotes a firm promise or oath, with Chiguiri and chico as Japanese glosses. Faint marks above chico’s final o do not establish an accent’s shape; the unaccented draft is retained as a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.
Juramento completes the oath gloss, after which the entry adds close friendship. Estrei- is divided from ta below; its provisional st spelling is not globally regularized.
Ta completes estreita. Meixei tagǒ coto nacare prohibits departing from the pledged agreement; Portuguese Não starts the translation continued below.

runs.text: diſcrepeis da promeßa que firmemẽte fizeſtes.

lines.note: The translation says not to depart from the promise firmly made. The nasal abbreviation in firmemẽte and the printed promeßa are retained.
Meixeqi is a distinguished or excellent stone, paraphrased Na aruixi. Excellẽte, not excallẽte, is supported by the scan; the abbreviation is not expanded.
Meixi denotes an excellent teacher or master. Its unmarked spelling remains distinct from nearby Meixǒ entries; no accent is supplied by analogy.
Meixo and Nadocoro concern an excellent or celebrated place. Afama- has f rather than long ſ and completes afamado below.
Do lugar completes the celebrated-place definition. Secretas is an additional noun gloss, understood here as privies, not an adjective meaning “secret famous places.”
This Meixǒ is an eminent commander, paraphrased Qicoye aru taixǒ. Both visible carons are retained, and afa- continues below.
Mado completes afamado, while bom adds the commander’s excellence. This closes the military sense before the separate master-or-scholar homophone.
The second Meixǒ denotes a good, learned master. It is a separate homophone from the preceding commander and is not merged with that definition.
Meixu, paraphrased Nano xujin, is a good lord or king. Both bõ forms retain their nasal abbreviation; Rey keeps its printed capitalization.
This Meixu is a precious stone. The example begins Meixuuo xi-, with an attached object particle and the verb divided across rows.

Razareba completes the condition of not recognizing the jewel; the rest treats it instead as guariacu, ordinary rubble or tile. The historical guariacu spelling and the upright citation label Xix. are retained.

runs.text: Não ſabendo o valor da pedra precioſa fica

lines.note: The Portuguese begins the same condition: without knowing the precious stone’s value, it ends up being treated as something else. Fica governs the continuation below.

runs.text: ſendo como qualquer pedra, ou telha: acom-

lines.note: The jewel is treated like any ordinary stone or tile. Acom- starts the following explanatory clause applying the comparison figuratively.

runs.text: modaſe aos que não conhecem a virtude, &c.

lines.note: Modaſe completes acomodaſe: the saying applies to people who fail to recognize virtue. This moral application belongs to the jewel example, not the wine entry below.
The next Meixu is a renowned, excellent drink, paraphrased Na aru ſaqe. Vinho is the dictionary’s gloss and need not imply grape wine specifically; excel- continues below.
Lente completes excellente and closes the renowned-drink definition. This damaged short continuation remains distinct from the next headword.
Meixun, paraphrased Aquru faru, is the new year or spring that is beginning. Pri- is the first part of primavera, continued below.
Mauera completes primavera, and que começa specifies the newly beginning season. The row closes this seasonal entry.
Meiyacu is a good remedy, explained by Meiyono cuſuri and Boa mezinha. Historical mezinha is not replaced with a modern medical term.
Meiyen is a good, renowned garden. Compact &nomeado spacing is retained; S. is distinguished as the upright written-usage label.
Meiyo concerns honour, praise, or a celebrated name, paraphrased Nano fomare. The Portuguese adjective celebre is divided after ce-.
Lebre completes celebre. Meiyouo nocoſu means leaving an honoured name behind; Deixar grã- has an abbreviation and a visible terminal hyphen.
The wholly italic de nome completes grã-de nome, “a great name.” OCR Ne is not Japanese. Continuation indentation is restored without changing the physical row’s ID.
Meiyono is an attributive expression for something distinguished or renowned. Its example follows rather than ending the entry at italic Vt.
Meiyono fito is a distinguished person, translated as a great and eminent man. The final vowel is visibly o, not OCR Meiyone.

runs.text: Tingir de certo modo, & laya dei-

lines.note: Meiyui describes patterned dyeing. The Portuguese reads de certo modo, “in a certain way,” not cento; dei- begins deixando below.

runs.text: xando hũs brancos a que não chega a tinta.

lines.note: Xando completes deixando: white areas remain where dye does not reach. The gloss explains the resulting pattern without establishing a particular modern process.
Meizan is a renowned mountain, paraphrased Na aru yama. Nomeado describes its reputation rather than an instruction to name it.

runs.text: Liuro que trata de muitos offi-

lines.note: Meizucuxi names a book dealing with many craftsmen. Offi- continues below, where the sword-making context specifies the artisans.
Ciaes completes officiaes, here sword-making craftsmen rather than military officers. Catanas is italic in this impression.
Memaje denotes signalling with the eyes by blinking or winking. Compact deolho is retained, and the example repeats the headword across the break after Me-.
Majeuo completes Memajeuo ſuru, “to signal with the eyes.” A synonymous example begins with Me- at the row’s far end.

The continuation retains guuayeùo, giving the synonymous eye-signalling expression across the preceding Me- break. Final crop enlargement clearly shows two u types after g; the small grave-like mark over the later u is compatible with the aligned draft and is retained as a nonblocking graphic uncertainty, rather than regularizing the unfamiliar spelling.

runs.text: Doença de andar a cabeça à roda,

lines.note: Memaiqe describes dizziness, expressed as the head going round. Final à roda is Portuguese; the alternative symptom follows below.

runs.text: ou ſe ir o lume dos olhos.

lines.note: The second description is dimming or loss of the light of the eyes. It belongs to the dizziness entry and is not necessarily permanent blindness.

runs.text: Ter esta doença, ou a peſſoa

lines.note: Memaiqena refers to having the preceding condition or to a person who has it. The relative clause continues below, and the provisional esta typography is retained.
Que a tem completes “the person who has it,” with a referring to the illness. The short row is genuine body text.
Memixe is equated with Tecaqe and glossed Manceba, here a mistress or concubine. This Japanese synonym after i is not a Portuguese-embedded font-toggle term.
Memixemono has the same meaning as Memixe. Final X. is an upright regional-usage label, not part of italic Idem.
Men first means the face or a person’s presence, paraphrased Vomote. Rosto retains the provisional st reading, and Vt introduces the example below.
Menni and menuo motte are alternatives for speaking in person; prospective mǒſǒzu matches Direi, “I shall say.” L is the alternative marker, not Japanese.

runs.text: em preſença, ou quando me vir cem voſco.

lines.note: The translation completes “in person, or when I meet with you.” The scan appears to print anomalous cem voſco; cem is retained rather than silently regularized to expected com.
Mento vqetamauatta means hearing something directly or in person. Ouui begins the corresponding Portuguese translation; pre- continues below.

runs.text: ſença, ou de roſto a roſto. ¶ Item, Maſ-

lines.note: The translation finishes “in person, or face to face.” A second sense then begins with Maſ-, the start of the Portuguese word for a mask.
Cara completes Maſcara. Menuo caquru exemplifies putting on a mask; Por is the infinitive corresponding to modern pôr, not the preposition alone.

This Men denotes pardon or remission. The scan supports Yuruſu and abbreviated ſẽpre rather than Yuraſu and ſe pre. Go is a complete roman Japanese combining element within the Portuguese explanation.
The explanation allows Go or another compound element. Gomenno rinxi begins an example about an official order granting pardon; its object particle and verb continue below.
The verb completes the granting of the pardon order. Taif. is a single upright citation label; Lib. 36. is the italic book reference, including the visible final stop.

runs.text: Dando lhe carta, ou patente de perdão. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese gives a letter or patent of pardon. Go- then starts Gomen are, a separate request for forgiveness.
Men are completes Gomen are, “forgive me.” Menuo cô introduces a request for remission of a land obligation; its circumflexed ô is retained.

runs.text: Pedir o laurador ao ſenhor que lhe remita algũa

lines.note: A cultivator asks his lord to remit something. This explains the fiscal sense of men rather than another general interpersonal apology.

runs.text: couſa do rendimento da terra que està ja a va-

lines.note: The remission concerns the assessed return from land. The visible separation a va- is retained across the division of avaliada rather than respaced into modern orthography.
Liada completes avaliada, assessed by others. Menuo yaru gives the complementary action of granting remission, translated after Dar.

runs.text: eſta quita, como ſe ouuera de pagar 10. per-

lines.note: A numerical example supposes ten would otherwise be payable. Per- begins perdoar below; the numeral and its stop are preserved.

runs.text: doar lhe dous, & que pague oito.

lines.note: Doar completes perdoar: two are remitted and eight remain payable. These figures explain quita and are not a separate headword.
Menbacu is covering or binding the face, marked as written usage by upright S. Provisional rosto typography is not globally changed.
Ruixet menbacu is explained as being bound. Ruixet’s final t is the historical checked-coda spelling and is not expanded.

Menban is equated with Vguyſu, the Japanese singing bird compared here with a nightingale. Enlargement supports g, not OCR p, and the visible introductory i,; the printed uy sequence is not modernized.
Menbǒ, paraphrased Mugui bǒ, is a round wooden rod for preparing dough. Both carons are visible; its function continues below.

runs.text: batem, & eſtendem a maßa de que fazem

lines.note: The rod beats and spreads dough from which noodles are made. Printed maßa and eſtendem are retained without normalizing their s-types.
A letria completes the noodles description. This short row belongs to the rolling-pin definition, not Menbocu below.
Menbocu means honour. Menbocu mini begins the expression about honours exceeding one’s own deserts or station, completed by amaru below.
Amaru completes the first honour example, rendered as having very great honours. The next example starts with wholly roman Mẽ-; its abbreviation is not an isolated italic character.
Bocuuo completes abbreviated Menbocuuo, followed by fodocoſu. The Portuguese gives acquiring honour and praise; lou continues below without a visible terminal hyphen.
Uor completes louuor. Menbocuuo vxinǒ gives the opposite action, losing honour; the long-o mark is retained and the Portuguese object continues below.
Honra completes Perder a honra. This short continuation closes the paired gain-and-loss examples.
Menchǒ is paraphrased Vomoteuo vtçu, striking the face. The Portuguese begins with fist blows and adds another kind below.
The second alternative is slapping the face. Final S. is the upright written-usage label, not part of the italic sentence.
Mencu is dirt on the face, matching Vomoteno aca. The next example instructs someone to wash it off.
Mencuuo xendacu xeyo means washing the face. The Portuguese imperative begins Lauai, with L rather than OCR I; ro- continues below.
Sto completes rosto, followed by upright S. Far-right Mendan anticipates f316’s first entry and is separated as a catchword under a fresh ID, rather than retained in this gloss.
